In mathematics, '''Serre''' and '''localizing subcategories''' form important classes of [[Subcategory|subcategories]] of an [[abelian category]]. Localizing subcategories are certain Serre subcategories. They are strongly linked to the notion of a [[quotient category]].

== Serre subcategories ==

Let <math>\mathcal{A}</math> be an [[abelian category]]. A non-empty full [[subcategory]] <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is called a ''Serre subcategory'' (or also a ''dense subcategory''), if for every short [[exact sequence]] <math>0\rightarrow
A' \rightarrow A\rightarrow A''\rightarrow 0</math> in <math>\mathcal{A}</math> the object <math>A</math> is in <math>\mathcal{C}</math> if and only if the objects <math>A'</math>
and <math>A''</math> belong to <math>\mathcal{C}</math>. In words: <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is closed under subobjects, quotient objects
and extensions.

Each Serre subcategory <math>\mathcal{C}</math> of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is itself an abelian category, and the inclusion functor <math>\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{A}</math> is [[Exact functor|exact]]. The importance of this notion stems from the fact that kernels of [[exact functor|exact functors]] between abelian categories are Serre subcategories, and that one can build (for locally small <math>\mathcal{A}</math>) the [[Quotient of an abelian category|quotient category]] (in the sense of [[Pierre Gabriel|Gabriel]], [[Alexander Grothendieck|Grothendieck]], [[Jean-Pierre Serre|Serre]]) <math>\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{C}</math>, which has the same objects as <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, is abelian, and comes with an exact functor (called the quotient functor) <math>T\colon\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{C}</math> whose kernel is <math>\mathcal{C}</math>.

== Localizing subcategories ==

Let <math>\mathcal{A}</math> be locally small. The Serre subcategory <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is called ''localizing'' if the quotient functor
<math>T\colon\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{C}</math> has a
[[Adjoint functors|right adjoint]]
<math>S\colon\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}</math>. Since then <math>T</math>, as a left adjoint, preserves [[Limit (category theory)|colimits]], each localizing subcategory is closed under colimits. The functor <math>T</math> (or sometimes <math>ST</math>) is also called the ''localization functor'', and <math>S</math> the ''section functor''. The section functor is [[exact functor|left-exact]] and [[Full and faithful functors|fully faithful]].

If the abelian category <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is moreover
[[complete category|cocomplete]] and has [[injective hull|injective hulls]] (e.g. if it is a [[Grothendieck category]]), then a Serre
subcategory <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is localizing if and only if
<math>\mathcal{C}</math> is closed under arbitrary coproducts (a.k.a.
direct sums). Hence the notion of a localizing subcategory is
equivalent to the notion of a hereditary [[Torsion theory|torsion class]].

If <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is a Grothendieck category and <math>\mathcal{C}</math> a localizing subcategory, then <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and the quotient category
<math>\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{C}</math> are again Grothendieck categories.

The [[Gabriel-Popescu theorem]] implies that every Grothendieck category is the quotient category of a [[category of modules|module category]] <math>\operatorname{Mod}(R)</math> (with <math>R</math> a suitable [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]]) modulo a localizing subcategory.
